items.question: What two questions does IAM answer for every AWS account?
options: Who can get in, and what they are allowed to do
Which Region is cheapest, and which AMI to pick
How many VPCs to create, and which subnet is public
When to scale EC2, and how to set a billing alarm
items.ren_hint_tanglish: IAM = WHO get in + WHAT they can do.
items.explanation: IAM controls identity (who) and access (what). Users, roles, and policies exist to answer those two questions.

items.question: An EC2 server needs to read files from an S3 bucket. What should you use?
options: An IAM Role assumed by the EC2 instance (no long-lived password on the server)
An IAM User password hardcoded in a text file on the server
The root account access keys stored in the application
Share one teammate's login with the whole EC2 fleet
items.ren_hint_english: Services get Roles — never hardcode user credentials on machines.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: Service/machine-ku Role — server-la password store pannaadheenga.
items.explanation: Roles give temporary credentials. Hardcoded IAM User keys on a server are a classic breach path.

items.question: What is the most dangerous default when onboarding a new developer?
options: Giving them AdministratorAccess 'to make things easy for now'
Creating a scoped IAM User for their job
Attaching a least-privilege policy for one S3 bucket
Putting them in a team Group with shared read-only access
items.ren_hint_english: AdminAccess means they can delete production — least privilege first.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: AdministratorAccess = full control — least privilege thaan correct.
items.explanation: AdministratorAccess is full control. If they make a mistake (or credentials leak), blast radius is the whole account.

items.situation: A new mobile-backend developer starts tomorrow. They need read/write to one S3 bucket (mobile-app-assets) and permission to view EC2 in ap-south-1 — nothing else.
items.question: What is the correct IAM setup order?
options: Create IAM User → create a scoped Policy → attach Policy to the User (or Group)
Give them root login and change the password later
Share an existing developer's credentials for the first month
Skip IAM and open all S3 buckets to the public
items.ren_hint_english: User for login, Policy for permissions, attach — scoped to need only.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: User create → scoped Policy → attach. Need mattum, more illa.
items.explanation: One User per human, one Policy scoped to exact needs, then attach. That is least privilege in practice.

items.situation: A contractor finished a 3-month project last week. Their IAM User still exists and credentials still work.
items.question: What do you do first, then second?
options: Disable the IAM User immediately, then rotate or delete credentials
Wait until next quarter's access review
Give them AdministratorAccess as a thank-you
Change only the account alias and leave the user active
items.ren_hint_english: Access off first — every extra day is unnecessary risk.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: First disable — access cut pannunga. Apram credentials cleanup.
items.explanation: Disable same day to cut access while keeping audit history. Then clean up credentials. Never leave ex-contractors active.

items.situation: A developer says they cannot open an S3 bucket. Before you can help in the right place, you need the unique address of their company's AWS account.
items.question: What must you collect first? (Type the term.)
items.ren_hint_english: Building address of the AWS account — not the user's password.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: AWS account-oda unique address = Account ID.
items.explanation: Account ID uniquely identifies which AWS account you are working in. IAM User ID is who is inside that account.
